topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI literacy gap: mixed-methods evidence from employers on workforce readiness and curriculum priorities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on employer sample size, sectors, and geographic distribution — unclear from snippet. Findings on curriculum priorities may reflect dominant sectors in the sample rather than universal workforce needs.
takeaways: Identify specific AI literacy gaps your employees face by consulting directly with line managers and teams about which AI skills matter most to their roles — don't assume generic curricula will address real workplace priorities.

Use employer feedback to design targeted upskilling programmes that prioritise the AI competencies your organisation actually needs, rather than broad technical training that may not transfer to job performance.

Assess your current curriculum or training offerings against employer-identified priorities to find misalignments — this mixed-methods approach suggests combining surveys with qualitative feedback yields richer insights than either method alone.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; frameworks and competencies may have limited direct applicability to Australian organisational settings, though core digital literacy principles could transfer.
takeaways: Review identifies key digital competencies needed in public health; consider which of these competencies are most critical for your organisation's AI readiness and map them to current capability gaps.

European framework approach suggests structuring AI literacy around specific role-based competency clusters rather than generic training — tailor to your employees' actual job functions to increase relevance and uptake.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires translation and adaptation.
takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, helping learners develop interconnected skills across data literacy, critical thinking, and responsible use.

A holistic approach to AI education at foundational levels (middle school) may inform how organisations should structure AI upskilling programmes — integrating technical understanding with ethical reasoning and practical application.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education; findings may not generalise across other disciplines or non-academic settings. Geographic scope and sample size unclear from title/snippet.
takeaways: Design faculty development programmes that acknowledge and address resistance to AI adoption, positioning upskilling as a pathway from scepticism to practical readiness rather than top-down mandate.

Treat educators as a critical leverage point for AI literacy — their comfort and competence directly shapes how students engage with AI tools, making instructor training a prerequisite for institutional AI capability development.

Create structured, evidence-based faculty development that moves beyond abstract AI concepts to demonstrate real-world public health applications, helping educators model AI literacy in domain-specific contexts.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience and surveys, likely reflective of large multinational organisations but may not represent SMEs, non-profit sectors, or regions with different labour market dynamics.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will be most affected by generative AI adoption, then prioritise upskilling programmes for those employee groups to prevent skills obsolescence.

Design reskilling pathways that combine technical AI literacy (prompt engineering, AI tool use) with complementary soft skills (critical thinking, change management) rather than treating them separately.

Create visible internal communication about upskilling opportunities and career progression linked to AI capabilities — employees are more likely to engage with development if they see a clear connection to job security and advancement.

articles.title: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design - Frontiers
articles.snippet: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on materials science and informatics education context; applicability to broader organisational AI literacy programmes requires adaptation.
takeaways: Align AI literacy curriculum to actual work processes and domain workflows rather than teaching AI concepts in isolation — this improves both comprehension and transfer to practice.
Build in explicit training on scientific judgment and critical evaluation of AI outputs, not just technical skills — this helps employees make defensible decisions when using AI tools.
Consider equity implications when designing AI literacy programmes, ensuring all learners can engage regardless of prior technical background or access to resources.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot determine from title and snippet alone — geographic scope, sample size, sector, and methodology are not indicated in the provided information.
takeaways: AI adoption in organizations can both enhance and inhibit employee creativity depending on implementation context — assess whether your AI rollout is designed to augment creative thinking or inadvertently constrain it through over-automation or reduced autonomy.

Consider the 'double-edged' mechanisms: identify which organizational conditions (e.g., job control, task variety, collaborative norms) might amplify positive versus negative effects of AI on your team's creative output.

articles.title: Transforming work or eroding social capital? How reliance on artificial intelligence drives workplace involution - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Transforming work or eroding social capital? How reliance on artificial intelligence drives workplace involution  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited until full article reviewed — title suggests theoretical analysis of AI-driven workplace dynamics, but generalisability depends on research design (empirical study vs. conceptual framework) and participant demographics.
takeaways: Monitor whether AI adoption in your organisation is reducing face-to-face collaboration and informal knowledge-sharing networks — 'workplace involution' (inward-focused, repetitive work) can erode the social bonds that drive innovation and psychological safety.

When implementing AI systems, intentionally design touchpoints that maintain human connection and cross-team dialogue, rather than optimising for pure efficiency — this protects organisational culture and employee engagement alongside productivity gains.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature

The causal pathway proposed (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety/ethical leadership → depression) requires replication across different organisational contexts and geographies.
takeaways: AI adoption can harm employee wellbeing if it erodes psychological safety or ethical leadership; proactively reinforce both during AI implementation to protect mental health outcomes.

Monitor psychological safety and ethical leadership as leading indicators of negative employee mental health during AI transitions — these are actionable levers leaders can strengthen to mitigate depression risk.
Frame AI adoption with explicit ethical guardrails and transparent decision-making to maintain trust; absence of these practices may compound adoption stress and psychological distress.

articles.title: Deploying AI into workplaces: What leaders need to know - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Deploying AI into workplaces: What leaders need to know  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on APA expertise and US workplace psychology research, but recommendations should be adapted to Australian employment law, enterprise agreements, and cultural context.
takeaways: Establish clear governance structures before AI deployment: define roles, accountability, and decision-making authority to prevent confusion and resistance among staff.
Prioritise transparent communication about AI's purpose, limitations, and impact on roles — research shows this reduces anxiety and builds trust during technological transitions.
Assess psychological safety and existing team dynamics before introducing AI tools; poorly implemented AI in low-trust environments can amplify conflict and disengagement.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. Framework applies conceptually across sectors, but effectiveness may vary based on organizational context, AI implementation maturity, and employee demographics.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger both approach (seeking new opportunities with AI tools) and avoidance (withdrawing from AI-related tasks) behaviors in employees — understanding which tendency dominates in your organization helps tailor adoption support and training.

Job crafting interventions may need to explicitly address employees' emotional and motivational responses to AI, not just technical capability, to shift avoidance patterns toward constructive engagement with new tools.
Monitor for divergent responses to AI rollout within your workforce; some employees may proactively reshape their roles while others retreat, requiring differentiated change management strategies.

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed without access to full methodology. The Nature publication suggests peer-reviewed research, but geographic scope, sample characteristics, and sector coverage are unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Self-efficacy with AI tools may be a key lever for protecting employee mental health during AI adoption — assess and build confidence in your team's AI capabilities alongside change management efforts.

Mental health risks during AI implementation warrant proactive monitoring; consider screening for anxiety or stress related to AI tool adoption and provide targeted support for employees with lower AI self-efficacy.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are based on consulting experience but lack transparent methodology, sample details, or peer review. Findings likely reflect practices in large organisations across multiple sectors, but applicability to smaller Australian organisations or specific industries unclear.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (a one-time event) to 'AI adaptation' (ongoing behavioural change) to sustain engagement and performance as systems evolve.

Target specific human behaviours needed for AI success (e.g., comfort with ambiguity, continuous learning, cross-functional collaboration) rather than focusing solely on technical training or tool competence.

Design change initiatives around how people actually work, not how they 'should' work — resistance often signals misalignment between AI implementation and existing workflows or psychological safety concerns.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet alone. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings may be limited by sample geography and organisational context.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger either approach behaviours (employees proactively redesigning tasks to leverage AI) or avoidance behaviours (withdrawing from AI-related work) — recognising which response employees exhibit helps managers provide targeted support and reframing.

Job crafting interventions during AI rollout should address both motivational drivers (opportunity, autonomy) and emotional barriers (fear, uncertainty) to shift employees toward constructive engagement rather than passive resistance.

Early identification of avoidance patterns allows HR and managers to intervene before disengagement solidifies — brief coaching on AI utility and autonomy in task redesign can help reorient employees toward problem-solving.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's perspective reflects practices among large enterprises and multinational clients, but specific applicability depends on organisation size, sector, and geography; limited detail provided in snippet to assess methodological rigour.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a people challenge, not just a technology challenge — workforce readiness, role redesign, and capability building must be central to your AI strategy from the outset.

Align AI transformation initiatives with structured workforce development programs that address skill gaps, role transitions, and change management, rather than treating technology deployment and people changes as separate workstreams.
Identify early which employee groups will experience the largest role shifts and design targeted upskilling or redeployment pathways to maintain engagement and reduce resistance during AI rollout.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, but specific case studies and contexts not detailed in snippet. Findings likely reflect practices among large organisations and may not fully generalise to SMEs or public sector.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as organisational change management, not just technical training — this positions it as a strategic priority requiring executive sponsorship and change infrastructure rather than a standalone L&D initiative.

Design upskilling programs that address both skill gaps and mindset shifts, since resistance to AI adoption often stems from uncertainty and loss-of-control concerns that training alone won't resolve.

Align AI capability development with explicit business outcomes and role-specific applications, so employees see direct relevance and can apply learning immediately — this increases adoption and reduces attrition of newly trained staff.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without empirical data or defined sample. Insights may reflect US higher education and tech-sector biases rather than broader workforce populations.
takeaways: Identify which job roles in your organisation are most susceptible to AI disruption, then proactively design reskilling or role-redesign interventions for affected employees before change is forced.

Create transparent communication channels about how AI will affect individual roles — employees who understand the trajectory of change are more likely to engage with upskilling than those left uncertain.

articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature

Design AI rollouts to prioritize psychological safety and competence-building before deployment, as self-efficacy acts as a buffer against anxiety and stress during technology transitions.
Monitor mental health indicators during AI adoption phases, targeting support especially for employees with lower baseline self-efficacy to prevent disengagement or burnout.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — a news summary of research findings without details on study design, sample composition, or methodology; cannot assess applicability without access to the original research.
takeaways: The finding challenges the long-held assumption that personality is roughly half nature and half nurture, suggesting genetics may play a larger role than the classic 50/50 split.

If personality traits are more heritable than thought, it raises an intriguing question: how much of what we perceive as 'personal growth' through self-help or therapy actually reflects working within our genetic predispositions rather than fundamentally changing them.

This could explain why some personality traits feel remarkably stable across a person's lifetime — you might be fighting less against yourself and more with yourself when trying to change ingrained patterns.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet; likely limited to specific population and experimental conditions.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising moments in distinctly different ways — some personalities may lock in unexpected events vividly while others let them slip away.
Your personality type isn't just about how you act; it shapes what sticks in your memory, suggesting our traits fundamentally alter how we encode and store experiences.
This finding bridges personality psychology and memory research in a counterintuitive way: the 'big five' matters not just for behaviour but for which moments feel worth remembering.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research on social connection and health outcomes across diverse populations, though specific cultural contexts may influence friendship patterns and health mechanisms.
takeaways: Strong friendships have measurable biological effects: people with close social ties show better immune function, lower inflammation, and reduced cardiovascular disease risk — it's not just feeling good, your body literally responds to connection.
Social isolation is as harmful to longevity as smoking or obesity — a counterintuitive finding that shows friendship isn't a luxury but a health necessity on par with physical wellness habits.

Quality matters more than quantity: a few genuine friendships produce greater health benefits than a large shallow social network, so your intimate circle is doing more protective work than you might realise.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Limited specificity from snippet alone; likely synthesises psychological research on true crime consumption across multiple studies, though geographic scope and population diversity unclear.
takeaways: True crime fascination taps into psychological needs like sense-making, vicarious thrill-seeking, and feeling safer by studying others' misfortunes — the 'benign masochism' of consuming danger from a safe distance.
People aren't morbidly weird for binge-watching true crime: it's a normal psychological response tied to curiosity, pattern recognition, and our evolved need to learn from others' mistakes.

The appeal varies by personality — some seek narrative closure and justice, others get a dopamine hit from puzzle-solving, making true crime a window into how different minds process risk and morality differently.

articles.title: Traits that make someone seem more intellectual can also make them seem less liberal, study suggests - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Traits that make someone seem more intellectual can also make them seem less liberal, study suggests  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess from snippet alone — insufficient detail on methodology, sample size, or geographic scope provided.
takeaways: People unconsciously associate intellectual traits (like analytical thinking or precision) with political conservatism, even though intelligence and political ideology are independent.
This perception gap matters socially: appearing 'intellectual' may inadvertently signal political leanings to others, potentially affecting how ideas are received in diverse groups.
The finding is counterintuitive because we typically think of intellectualism as politically neutral — revealing how deeply stereotypes shape our snap judgments of others.

articles.title: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet provided; the full article would be needed to determine sample size, geographic scope, and methodological details.
takeaways: Your personality isn't just psychological — it has measurable physical correlates in your brain's structure, suggesting personality differences are rooted in actual neurological differences rather than purely learned behaviour.

This bridges the nature-versus-nurture debate in an interesting way: brain structure variations associated with personality traits hint that who you are has a biological foundation, not just environmental shaping.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and industry composition, which are not evident from the title and snippet. The causal pathway between AI adoption, psychological safety, and depression may vary significantly across organisational contexts, sectors, and cultural settings.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent attention to psychological safety and ethical leadership may increase employee mental health risks — assess your team's sense of safety during AI implementation, not just adoption metrics.

Ethical leadership practices and transparent communication about AI's role and limitations are protective factors during technological change — model these explicitly when introducing AI tools to reduce anxiety and disengagement.
Monitor psychological safety proactively during AI rollouts through check-ins or pulse surveys; depression and disengagement may surface as delayed effects rather than immediate resistance.

articles.title: Deploying AI into workplaces: What leaders need to know - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Deploying AI into workplaces: What leaders need to know  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — APA guidance reflects US workplace context and may not fully account for Australian employment law, cultural norms, or regulatory frameworks (e.g., Fair Work Act, privacy requirements). Principles around psychological safety are likely transferable, but specific recommendations should be adapted.
takeaways: Leaders should proactively communicate AI deployment plans, rationale, and expected impacts on roles to reduce uncertainty and anxiety—a key driver of psychological unsafety during technological change.

Establish clear governance structures and transparent decision-making processes around AI use to help employees understand how systems will be evaluated, monitored, and modified—critical for maintaining trust.

Create psychological safety explicitly by inviting employee feedback on AI implementation, addressing concerns without dismissal, and demonstrating that speaking up about risks or problems is valued and acted upon.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited specificity — typical BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but without access to full methodology, scope, and sample details, generalisability cannot be fully assessed. Findings may reflect BCG's client base rather than broader workforce populations.
takeaways: Psychological safety reduces barriers to participation and contribution, creating more equitable opportunity for all employees to engage — assess whether quieter or less senior team members have genuine voice in your workplace.
Use this lens to audit team dynamics: does psychological safety explain performance gaps or unequal advancement, and what specific structural or leadership changes could level the playing field?

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but lacks peer-reviewed validation and may reflect consulting client bias toward larger organisations.
takeaways: Build psychological safety by framing AI as a tool that augments human capability rather than replaces workers — explicitly communicate this shift in messaging to reduce anxiety and resistance.
Create structured opportunities for employees to experiment with AI tools in low-stakes environments, as hands-on experience builds both competence and confidence in using AI systems effectively.
Establish clear feedback loops and support mechanisms so employees feel empowered to voice concerns about AI implementation without fear of judgment or career consequences.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad but subject to typical survey limitations — results reflect respondent perceptions at a single point in time and may be skewed toward larger economies and digitally connected workforces. PwC surveys often overweight developed nations.
takeaways: Use workforce survey data to benchmark psychological safety perceptions in your organisation against global trends — identify where your team's sense of security, trust in leadership, or fear of speaking up differs from peers, then target interventions accordingly.

Global 'fears' data can help you anticipate and address the specific anxieties your team faces (e.g. job displacement, unfair treatment, lack of voice) before they erode psychological safety — tailor your safety-building efforts to real, documented concerns rather than assumptions.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM's guidance reflects US HR practice standards, but core psychological safety principles are applicable across geographies. Implementation details may need adaptation for Australian workplace contexts and enterprise agreements.
takeaways: Identify the specific four leader behaviours SHRM recommends (likely including modelling vulnerability, responding non-defensively to concerns, and inviting input) and audit your own team interactions against these to establish a baseline before implementing changes.

Psychological safety is built through repeated demonstrations of safety rather than one-off initiatives—establish a 90-day accountability plan where you track consistent application of recommended behaviours and collect team feedback on perceived safety shifts.
